blocks.text: Sooner or later, a tool you want an AI model to use is not going to be sitting on the same machine as the model itself.

Maybe it is a company database only reachable from inside a data center, maybe it is a shared service a whole team relies on, maybe it is simply something too expensive or too sensitive to run a fresh copy of on every laptop.

Whenever a server lives somewhere else, MCP needs a transport that can cross that distance, and the most familiar way to do that is the same way almost everything on the web already works, plain HTTP.
1. HTTP as a Transport for MCP

blocks.alt: Client sends an HTTP request to a remote MCP server and gets a response
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785439738497-107721045.png

HTTP transport means exactly what it sounds like, the client sends an MCP message as the body of an HTTP request, and the server sends its reply back as the body of an HTTP response. Nothing about the JSON-RPC message format changes, a tools/call request looks the same whether it travels over stdio or over HTTP, only the outer envelope carrying it is different.
This matters because it means everything learned about MCP messages in earlier modules carries over directly, the new material in this lesson is entirely about the envelope, not the contents.

It is worth noticing early that HTTP transport does not change what a tool call means, only how the bytes describing it travel, a tools/call for get_weather is exactly the same JSON regardless of which transport delivers it.
2. Why a Remote Server Needs a Network Transport
STDIO only works when a host can spawn the server itself as a child process, which requires both sides to share a filesystem and an operating system.
A remote server breaks that assumption entirely, it might be running in a data center on another continent, managed by a different team, scaled across many machines.

The only way to reach it is across a network, and HTTP is the most universally supported, most firewall-friendly way to do that, every corporate network, every cloud provider, and every developer’s laptop already knows how to send an HTTP request.

HTTP also brings decades of surrounding tooling along with it for free, proxies, load balancers, API gateways, logging middleware, and browser developer tools all already understand HTTP, which means a remote MCP server can plug into infrastructure a team has likely already built for other services, rather than needing something bespoke.
3. Request-Response Shape Over HTTP

A typical MCP call over HTTP is a single POST request, with the JSON-RPC message as the request body, and the server’s JSON-RPC response coming back as the HTTP response body. This maps naturally onto how most web APIs already work, one request in, one response out, which is a large part of why HTTP was a natural second transport to standardize after stdio.

code.content:
POST /mcp HTTP/1.1
Host: tools.example.com
Content-Type: application/json

{"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 7, "method": "tools/call", "params": {"name": "get_weather", "arguments": {"city": "Mumbai"}}}

blocks.text: This one-request-in, one-response-out shape is exactly how most developers already think about calling a web API, which is part of why HTTP was a comfortable second transport for the ecosystem to adopt after stdio.
4. Where JSON-RPC Fits Inside an HTTP Request

blocks.alt: An HTTP request body carries a JSON-RPC payload
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785439738497-851238327.png

It helps to keep two layers clearly separate in your head, the outer HTTP layer, with its method, headers, and status code, and the inner JSON-RPC layer, with its own id, method, and params fields. HTTP does not know or care what jsonrpc, id, or method mean inside the body, as far as HTTP is concerned it is just delivering some bytes with a content type of application json, all of the MCP-specific meaning lives entirely inside that body.

code.content:
import requests

response = requests.post(
    "https://tools.example.com/mcp",
    json={"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 7, "method": "tools/call",
          "params": {"name": "get_weather", "arguments": {"city": "Mumbai"}}},
    headers={"Authorization": "Bearer sk-example-token"},
)
result = response.json()

blocks.text: Because of this clean separation, an ordinary HTTP proxy or logging tool can inspect and route an MCP request perfectly well without understanding anything about JSON-RPC at all, it only needs to treat the body as an opaque blob of JSON.
5. Choosing an Endpoint and HTTP Method

Most HTTP-based MCP servers expose a single endpoint, commonly something like slash mcp, that accepts POST requests for every kind of JSON-RPC message, rather than defining a separate URL path for every method the way a typical REST API might. The JSON-RPC method field inside the body is what actually distinguishes a tools/call from a resources/read, the URL path itself usually stays constant across every call to a given server.

blocks.title: Not a REST API underneath
blocks.content: Even though it travels over HTTP, an MCP endpoint is not meant to be browsed like a typical REST API with a different URL per resource, it is a single JSON-RPC endpoint carried on top of HTTP.

blocks.text: GET requests are sometimes used alongside POST in an MCP over HTTP deployment, most commonly to open a Server-Sent Events stream for server-initiated messages, a pattern covered in full in the dedicated SSE lesson later in this module, POST remains the workhorse for ordinary client-initiated JSON-RPC calls.
6. Headers That Matter for MCP Over HTTP

A handful of HTTP headers do real work in an MCP exchange. Content-Type tells the server the body is JSON. Authorization typically carries a bearer token or API key proving who is calling. A session identifier, often carried in a custom header, lets the server associate this particular request with an already-established MCP session, covered in more detail later in this lesson.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Header","Purpose"],"rows":[["Content-Type","Tells the server the request body is JSON"],["Authorization","Carries the credential proving who is making the call"],["Mcp-Session-Id","Associates this request with an existing MCP session"]]}

blocks.title: Custom headers vary by server
blocks.content: The exact name used for a session header is not universally fixed across every implementation, always check a given server’s documentation rather than assuming a single header name works everywhere.

blocks.text: 7. Handling One Request Per Call

Unlike a long-lived stdio pipe that stays open for an entire session, a plain HTTP request-response cycle is usually a fresh connection, or at least a fresh logical exchange, for every single call. A client calling three tools in a row typically makes three separate HTTP requests, each with its own request and response, rather than three messages flowing continuously over one already-open pipe.

code.content:
results = []
for tool_call in pending_calls:
    r = requests.post(endpoint, json=tool_call, headers=headers)
    results.append(r.json())

blocks.text: Some client libraries batch several JSON-RPC calls into a single HTTP request when the underlying protocol version supports batching, reducing the number of round trips, but this is an optimization on top of the basic pattern, not a change to the fundamental one-request-one-response shape.
8. Network Latency Compared to stdio

blocks.alt: Stdio latency is compared against HTTP network latency
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785439738498-875837819.png

Where a local pipe delivers a message in a fraction of a millisecond, an HTTP call to a remote server has to cross an actual network, DNS resolution if the connection is new, a TCP handshake, often a TLS handshake, and then the round trip itself, easily tens of milliseconds even to a nearby data center, and considerably more across a longer distance. This is not a flaw in HTTP, it is simply the physical cost of talking to something that is not in the same room.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Transport","Typical round trip"],"rows":[["stdio, local pipe","Well under one millisecond"],["HTTP, same region","Roughly ten to fifty milliseconds"],["HTTP, cross region or continent","Frequently over one hundred milliseconds"]]}

blocks.text: This does not mean HTTP is a poor choice, it means the two transports solve different problems, a tool that genuinely needs to run locally with minimal overhead should stay on stdio, while a tool that genuinely needs to live remotely accepts the network cost that comes with that requirement.

blocks.title: Latency budget
blocks.content: When designing a tool meant to be called many times in a tight loop by an AI agent, it is worth explicitly budgeting for HTTP round trip time, a workflow calling the same remote tool fifty times in sequence can accumulate seconds of pure network latency that a local stdio tool would never incur.

blocks.text: 9. Statelessness of HTTP Itself

blocks.alt: Request one and request two arrive at the server with no shared memory between them
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785439738711-224876762.png

HTTP was designed as a stateless protocol, each request is meant to carry everything the server needs to understand it, and the server is not required to remember anything about a previous request from the same client. This is exactly why cookies, tokens, and session identifiers exist in the wider web, they are all ways of layering state back on top of a protocol that fundamentally does not track it on its own.

This design choice is also exactly what makes HTTP so easy to scale horizontally, since no individual server needs to remember anything between requests, any available instance can handle any incoming request equally well.
10. The MCP Session Living Above the Stateless Protocol
An MCP session, the ongoing sequence of calls between one client and one server, is a concept that exists above HTTP, not inside it.

Even though every individual HTTP request is technically independent, the client and server still need to remember things across calls, what capabilities were negotiated during initialization, what tools are available, sometimes conversation-specific state.
HTTP transport carries each individual message just fine, but the session itself has to be tracked deliberately by the application layer sitting on top.

blocks.title: Two different kinds of state
blocks.content: Do not confuse HTTP connection state, like whether a TCP socket is open, with MCP session state, like whether initialization has already happened, the two are tracked completely separately.

blocks.text: This layering is a good general pattern to recognize, plenty of protocols built on top of HTTP add their own notion of session or state, cookies for a browser session, tokens for an API session, and MCP session identifiers work the same way conceptually.
11. Session Identifiers and How They're Carried

blocks.alt: A session id header links stateless requests back to one session
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785439738712-725638673.png

Since HTTP itself will not remember a client between requests, MCP servers over HTTP commonly issue a session identifier the first time a client initializes, and expect that identifier back on every subsequent request, usually in a header. The server uses that identifier purely to look up whatever session state it is holding on its side, negotiated capabilities, an open session context, anything established earlier in the conversation.

code.content:
# first call: initialize, server returns a session id
init_response = requests.post(endpoint, json=init_request)
session_id = init_response.headers["Mcp-Session-Id"]

# every later call includes it
requests.post(endpoint, json=tool_call, headers={"Mcp-Session-Id": session_id})

blocks.text: If a session identifier is lost, forgotten, or expired, the server typically treats the next request as belonging to a brand new session, which usually means the client needs to run initialization again before anything else will succeed, exactly the kind of edge case reconnection logic, covered later in this module, needs to account for.
12. Authentication Needs That Don't Exist for stdio

blocks.alt: Stdio needs no auth while HTTP needs tokens or keys
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785439738713-505850316.png
A local stdio server never had to prove who was calling it, the operating system already guaranteed that only the process that spawned it could write to its stdin.
A remote HTTP server has no such guarantee, anyone who can reach its network address can attempt to send it a request, so authentication becomes mandatory rather than optional.

A full treatment of authentication schemes, API keys, OAuth, and more, is covered later in the dedicated Authentication and Security module, this lesson only needs you to recognize that the need itself is new, introduced specifically by going remote.

Even a lightweight shared secret is far better than nothing for a remote endpoint, leaving a remote MCP server completely open on the network is one of the most common early mistakes teams make when moving a tool from local to remote for the first time.
13. Error Handling and HTTP Status Codes
HTTP transport gives you two layers of error signaling at once, the HTTP status code, and the JSON-RPC error object inside the body.
A request that never reaches the server correctly, bad authentication, a malformed body, a server that is down, tends to show up as a non-2xx status code.
A request that reaches the server fine but fails at the MCP level, an unknown tool name, invalid arguments, shows up as a normal 200 status carrying a JSON-RPC error object in the body instead.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Failure kind","Where it shows up"],"rows":[["Invalid or missing credentials","HTTP 401 or 403 status code"],["Server unreachable or down","Connection failure or 5xx status code"],["Unknown tool name at the MCP level","200 status, with a JSON-RPC error object in the body"]]}

blocks.text: 14. Connection Reuse and Keep-Alive at the HTTP Layer

Opening a fresh TCP and TLS connection for every single request is wasteful, so most HTTP clients and servers reuse an underlying connection across multiple requests using HTTP keep-alive, avoiding repeated handshakes. This is a detail handled by the HTTP client library in most cases, but it is worth knowing it exists, since a client that accidentally disables connection reuse can see a surprising latency jump with no other code change at all.

code.content:
import requests
# a Session reuses the underlying connection across calls automatically
session = requests.Session()
session.post(endpoint, json=request_one)
session.post(endpoint, json=request_two)  # reuses the same TCP connection

blocks.text: Connection pooling becomes especially important for an AI agent that might call the same remote tool dozens of times in a single task, since the cost of repeatedly opening fresh connections would otherwise dominate the actual work being done.
15. Scaling Considerations for HTTP Servers

Because HTTP is stateless at its core, a well-designed remote MCP server can often run behind a load balancer with many identical server instances behind it, any instance can handle any incoming request as long as session state is stored somewhere shared, like a database or an in-memory store all instances can reach, rather than kept only in the memory of one specific process.
This is precisely the kind of horizontal scaling a local stdio server, tied permanently to one subprocess, could never offer.

This same statelessness is why many production deployments store session state in something like a shared cache or database rather than in a single server’s process memory, so that a request landing on a different instance than the one that handled initialization still finds the session data it needs.
16. When HTTP Transport Is the Right Choice

blocks.alt: Needing a remote server points toward choosing HTTP transport
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785439738713-192873840.png

HTTP transport is the right call whenever a server needs to be reachable from more than one machine, needs proper authentication, or benefits from being scaled and load balanced like any other web service.
It fits particularly well for tool calls that are relatively infrequent or independent of each other, where the overhead of a fresh request-response cycle each time is not a meaningful cost.
For servers that need to push frequent updates back to the client without the client asking first, the next lessons on WebSockets and Server-Sent Events cover better-suited alternatives.
17. HTTP Transport Alongside Other Remote Options

HTTP is rarely the only transport a remote MCP deployment supports, many servers accept plain HTTP for simple request-response calls while layering Server-Sent Events on top for anything the server needs to push proactively, giving clients a single base URL that quietly supports both patterns depending on what a given interaction needs.

Understanding plain HTTP thoroughly first makes both of the next two lessons easier, WebSockets and SSE are each best understood as HTTP plus one additional idea layered on top, rather than as something built from scratch.
Worked Example

Imagine a remote MCP server wrapping a company’s internal ticketing system, reachable at a fixed URL. A client first sends an initialize request, receives a session id back in a response header, then sends a tools/call request for create_ticket, including that session id on every request from here forward.

Notice how the session id, obtained once during initialization, is what ties this second, entirely separate HTTP request back to the same logical MCP session, even though HTTP itself treats the two requests as completely unrelated.

If the create_ticket call above needed to run again a few minutes later, the client would reuse the exact same session id already stored from initialization, only calling initialize again if the server had responded with a session-expired error in the meantime.
Common Mistakes

items: Assuming a session automatically persists across requests just because it is the same client, without explicitly sending the session identifier back on every call.
Treating every non-200 response the same way, instead of distinguishing an HTTP-level failure from a JSON-RPC-level error returned with a 200 status.
Opening a brand new connection for every single request instead of reusing a session or connection pool, quietly adding latency to every call.
Skipping authentication during early development and forgetting to add it back before a server becomes reachable outside a trusted local network.
Reaching for HTTP transport for a use case that really needs frequent server-initiated updates, where WebSockets or SSE would fit far better.

blocks.text: A closely related mistake worth calling out on its own, logging the full request body for debugging and accidentally capturing an Authorization header or session identifier in plaintext logs, quietly creating a security exposure.
Practice

Stand up the smallest possible HTTP server you can, one endpoint that accepts a POST request, reads a JSON-RPC message from the body, and returns a hardcoded JSON-RPC response. Then write a small client script that sends three separate tool calls to it in a row, printing the latency of each call. Add an Authorization header check on the server side that rejects any request missing a specific token, and confirm your client fails clearly when you temporarily remove that header.

code.content:
import time, requests
for i in range(3):
    start = time.time()
    r = requests.post(endpoint, json={"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": i, "method": "ping", "params": {}})
    print(i, time.time() - start, r.status_code)

items: As a stretch, add a small artificial delay to your server handler and measure how it changes the latency printed by your client.
Then simulate a dropped session by having your server occasionally return a 401 for the session header, and add logic to your client that reruns initialize when that happens.

blocks.text: Key Takeaway

HTTP transport lets an MCP client reach a server that cannot simply be spawned as a local subprocess, carrying the exact same JSON-RPC messages inside ordinary HTTP requests and responses. Because HTTP itself is stateless, an MCP session has to be tracked deliberately on top of it, usually through a session identifier sent back on every request, and going remote also introduces real authentication requirements that a local stdio server never needed.

The next lesson looks at WebSockets, a transport built to keep one connection open in both directions at once, useful when a server needs to push frequent updates to a client rather than only responding to requests the client initiates.
